title: Logical programs scheduled by the operating system
kicker: Operating system · logical circuits on every design
summary: Small logical circuits on distance-3 surface-code blocks, written as QSysASM without a single time. The operating system schedules each one, the timetable is compiled to RISC-Q firmware and run on the design's cycle-exact model, and every latency the hardware needed beyond what the OS was told is learned, until every operation of the program fits its window. 11 programs on 6 designs of three platforms.
method: Each program is a logical circuit written out at the physical level: every syndrome round requests 8 ancillas, routes each to its stabilizer's data qubits, entangles and measures them, and releases them; rounds are decoded by `decode_syndrome` and the correction applied with `pauli_frame_update`; logical CNOTs are transversal, and a magic state arrives by `request_magic` into a requested ancilla block with the factory's workspace. No statement carries a time.

The operating system first counts the design's capacities: qubits, gate slots (beams or channels), decoders, factories, movers, the readout channels, and on atoms and ions the beams and channels a factory borrows; the interface's machine line has no field for the last two. It is told only typical latencies for the platform. It then schedules the program (list scheduling, first ready first served, ancillas acquired in program order so that no schedule deadlocks). The timetable is placed on the design, compiled to firmware for every control core and run on the Lean model of RISC-Q, and each operation is checked against the window the OS gave it.

Every latency the hardware needed beyond the declared one is raised to what was measured (rounded to the controller's 2 ns or 10 ns grid) and the program is scheduled again. A program conforms when one run fits every window.

rows: One logical qubit, two syndrome rounds
A distance-3 surface-code block holds |0⟩ for two rounds of all eight stabilizers; the syndromes are decoded, the correction goes to the Pauli frame, and the block is read out.
Block 0 in |+⟩_L, block 1 in |0⟩_L, a round on each, a transversal CNOT, a round on each, then both read out in Z: the two logical outcomes agree.
Logical GHZ state of three blocks
Block 0 in |+⟩_L, two transversal CNOTs to blocks 1 and 2, a round on each block between and after, then all three read out in Z.
A Bell pair between blocks 1 and 2, a transversal CNOT from block 0 into block 1, block 0 read out in X and block 1 in Z, and the two outcomes corrected on block 2 through the Pauli frame.
Logical CNOT between two logical qubits
Two blocks prepared in |+⟩_L and |0⟩_L, a round on each, a transversal CNOT, a round on each, then block 0 read out in X and block 1 in Z.
A T gate by magic-state injection

A magic state |T⟩ requested from the factory into an ancilla block, a transversal CNOT from the data block into it, the magic block read out and released, and the outcome applied to the data block's frame.
Two logical qubits held side by side
Two independent blocks, each through two syndrome rounds, decoded and read out: the operating system interleaves them on shared services.
Logical SWAP from three transversal CNOTs
Block 0 in |+⟩_L and block 1 in |0⟩_L exchanged by CNOT 0→1, 1→0, 0→1, with a syndrome round on each block before and after; block 0 read out in Z and block 1 in X.
A logical Z⊗Z parity check through a third block
Blocks 0 and 1 in |+⟩_L, block 2 in |0⟩_L; transversal CNOTs from each into block 2 copy their Z⊗Z parity onto it, block 2 is read out, and its outcome is applied to block 1's frame.
Four logical qubits sharing one decoder
Four independent blocks, two syndrome rounds each, decoded and read out: every decode queues for the machine's decoders and every round for its ancillas.
Two T gates competing for one factory

Two magic states requested back to back for two data blocks; with one factory the second request waits for the first. Each is consumed by a transversal CNOT, read out, and applied to its block's frame.

findings: The schedule-then-measure loop converges in 2 or 3 runs on every design. Gate, measurement, decode and factory times do not depend on the schedule, so one run measures them; a route's time depends on where the qubits are, which the schedule changes (1 of 66 runs needed a third run for a longer route). The OS does not need to be told the hardware's latencies; it needs its capacities.

The interface's machine line has no field for readout concurrency. Atoms and ions have a fixed number of imaging or detection channels, and a schedule that measures more qubits at once than there are channels loses bits on the hardware. Counted on the design and given to the scheduler as a pool, the same programs conform (compare the last run above).

On atoms and ions a magic-state factory is not a separate machine: its checks run on the same addressing beams and readout channels as the program (8 of each at once for a distance-3 patch). The interface counts factories but not what they borrow; the OS reserves those beams and channels for as long as `request_magic` runs, and without that the program's gates and readouts find no free channel.

One route latency is not enough on atoms and ions: the time a route needs depends on where the qubits are, so different programs on the same design need different route latencies (166.8 µs – 223.6 µs on moving atoms, 1,054 µs – 1,628 µs on the trapped-ion QCCD). The OS has to declare the worst one, or schedule with positions.

A magic state takes 81.9 µs from the injection factory on the superconducting design and 2,075 µs on atoms; told 10 µs and 1 ms, the OS learns both from one run. With one factory, two T gates take 0.180 ms against 0.099 ms for one: the second request waits for the factory.
Every run is reproducible from its timetable alone: each run above shows the QSysASM the OS produced, and replaying that text on the same design gives the same run.
